## Introduction

This vignette shows how to use core dplyr verbs on FiveThirtyEight's recent college graduates dataset (<https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data/tree/master/college-majors>). Each row is a major, with pay, employment, and gender-mix figures.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

## 1. Load the data from a URL

```{r load}
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/college-majors/recent-grads.csv"
grads <- read_csv(url, show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(grads)
```

## 2. Select, rename, and drop missing rows

`select()` keeps the columns we need, `rename_with()` standardizes the names, and `drop_na()` removes the incomplete row(s).

```{r clean}
grads_clean <- grads |>
  select(Major, Major_category, Total, Men, Women, ShareWomen,
         Employed, Unemployed, Unemployment_rate,
         Median, P25th, P75th, College_jobs, Non_college_jobs) |>
  rename_with(str_to_lower) |>
  rename(share_women = sharewomen) |>
  drop_na()

nrow(grads); nrow(grads_clean)
```

## 3. Create new columns with `mutate()` and `case_when()`

```{r mutate}
grads_feat <- grads_clean |>
  mutate(
    college_job_share = college_jobs / (college_jobs + non_college_jobs),
    pay_spread        = p75th - p25th,
    pay_tier = case_when(
      median >= 60000 ~ "High",
      median >= 45000 ~ "Mid",
      .default = "Lower"
    ),
    gender_mix = case_when(
      share_women >= 0.6 ~ "Women-majority",
      share_women <= 0.4 ~ "Men-majority",
      .default = "Balanced"
    )
  )

grads_feat |> select(major, median, pay_tier, share_women, gender_mix) |> head()
```

## 4. Summarize by group with `across()`

`across()` applies the same function to several columns at once, and `.names` controls the output column names.

```{r summarise}
by_category <- grads_feat |>
  group_by(major_category) |>
  summarise(
    n_majors = n(),
    graduates = sum(total),
    across(c(median, unemployment_rate, college_job_share),
           \(x) mean(x), .names = "avg_{.col}"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_median))

by_category
```

## 5. Find top rows with `slice_max()`

Top five majors overall by median pay:

```{r slice-top}
grads_feat |>
  slice_max(median, n = 5) |>
  select(major, major_category, median, unemployment_rate)
```

Highest-paying major within each category (`slice_max()` respects grouping):

```{r slice-group}
grads_feat |>
  group_by(major_category) |>
  slice_max(median, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(major_category, major, median) |>
  arrange(desc(median))
```

## 6. Count combinations with `count()`

```{r count}
grads_feat |>
  count(gender_mix, pay_tier) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = pay_tier, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

## 7. Visualize the summary

```{r plot, fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
by_category |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_median, y = fct_reorder(major_category, avg_median))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Average Median Pay by Major Category",
       x = "Average median earnings", y = NULL)
```

The data cleaning process involved a combination of a few dplyr functions. We engineered the pay and gender_mixed variables, grouped by categories, and found the top performers. Engineering majors have high average pay, and the across function along with slice_max reduces repetitive coding significantly. Extensions include weighting by totals and comparing unemployment_rate by gender_mixed.
